extracted.intended_audience: law professors, scholars, patent attorneys, judges, and policymakers interested in patentable subject matter and business-method patents
extracted.subtask_description: Scholarly analysis of why business-method patents arose and how legal, administrative, and technological forces determine their patentability under U.S. law. Focuses on statutory text, PTO practice, Federal Circuit and Supreme Court doctrine (e.g., State Street, Alappat, Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory scope under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentable subject matter is defined by statute as “any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,” and the Act defines “process” to include “process, art, or method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly cites the statutory text as the baseline criterion: if an invention falls within one of these statutory categories (e.g., a process/method), it is prima facie within §101. The article emphasizes that the statutory language tends to cut against categorical exclusions (e.g., a blanket business-method exception) and that courts often return to the text when assessing scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness / usefulness (the “new and useful” requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute authorizes patents on “any new and useful process…,” so claimed inventions must be new and useful to qualify as patentable subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats novelty/usefulness as embedded in §101's language; lack of novelty has historically been invoked to reject claims (see discussion of prior cases). Novelty here is discussed as a separate ground (often §102), but the text notes earlier decisions rejected business-method patents on grounds like lack of novelty rather than a categorical business-method bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract idea exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have refused patents that claim mere 'abstract ideas'; several prior business-method rejections rested on the prohibition against patenting an 'abstract idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article identifies the 'abstract idea' doctrine as the practical limiting principle through which courts exclude unpatentable business methods. It explains that prior cases often relied on the abstract-idea prohibition rather than a distinct business-method exception, and that the Supreme Court has used the abstract-idea exception to limit business-method patentability where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not a mere abstraction / 'art' must be more than abstraction (Hotel Security Checking principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed 'art' or method must not be a mere abstraction; it must be an application of knowledge or means to accomplish a desired end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Hotel Security Checking Co. v. Lorraine Co., the article notes the guiding principle that, in patent law, 'an art is not a mere abstraction.' This functions as a substantive test for excluding claims that are only abstract concepts rather than concrete, applied techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test (Alappat/State Street formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process is patentable if it produces a 'useful, concrete and tangible result.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article identifies this test as central to State Street (and Alappat before it). It notes the widespread citation of this formulation but also records that later en banc Federal Circuit/Bilski developments rejected or limited the test. Usefulness: citation and historical role; caveat: later curtailed by higher court analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO administrative practice — historical 'method of doing business' entry in the MPEP
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the PTO's MPEP listed 'Method of Doing Business' as one of a few exceptions to patentable subject matter, though the agency recognized weaknesses in that position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article quotes the MPEP (First Edition) language: 'Method of Doing Business … the law is settled by the method of doing business can be rejected as not being within the statutory classes.' It explains three weaknesses in that position (thin authority, tension with statutory text, and that the MPEP only said such a method 'can be rejected' rather than must be).

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO Examination Guideline for Computer-Related Inventions (1996): treat business-method claims as process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO instructed that 'claims should not be categorized as methods of doing business' and that 'such claims should be treated like any other process claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights the 1996 guideline as an administrative rule changing examiner practice: instead of maintaining a separate 'business method' category, examiners were to examine such claims under the same statutory and doctrinal framework as other process claims (e.g., §101, novelty, obviousness). The PTO later issued a white paper and other guidance reinforcing that approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative classification and issuance as indicia of acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO's issuance of numerous patents in business-related subclasses (e.g., class 705/subclass 408) indicates administrative acceptance of business-method patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses PTO classification/issuance history (many issued patents in financial/management subclasses) as evidence that administrative practice effectively moved away from a categorical business-method bar. This functions as a practical criterion: whether the PTO has historically examined/issued patents in the field bears on admissibility and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive approach: textualism and statutory structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts' interpretive stance (e.g., textualism) influences whether business methods are treated as within §101; textualist readings of the Patent Act favor recognizing business-method patents where the text is broad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article argues that the Supreme Court's embrace of textualism (notably in Bilski) played a role in sustaining some business-method patentability by hewing to the statute's broad wording. This is a meta-criterion—judges' interpretive methods affect outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The role of external technological/industrial facts ('law followed technology')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the claimed subject matter reflects technological transformations (e.g., financial engineering, computing techniques) rather than mere business practices influences the law's treatment, because the rise of technology-driven business methods led the PTO and courts to treat them like other technological innovations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that as business fields adopted rigorous mathematical and engineering methods, they came to resemble technological fields; this practical reality led practitioners to seek patents and the legal system to adapt. Thus, an evaluative criterion is whether the invention applies technological means and produces engineering-like results rather than being solely a business or abstract concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior Federal Circuit en banc precedent (Alappat/Bilski lineage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower-court (Federal Circuit) en banc doctrines (e.g., Alappat's adoption of the 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' test; later en banc Bilski overruling/limiting such tests) guide patentability assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that State Street followed en banc precedent (Alappat), and that the Federal Circuit later revisited and limited those doctrines en banc in Bilski. Practitioners must therefore evaluate patentable-subject-matter issues against the current controlling Federal Circuit en banc pronouncements and how they align with Supreme Court guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits via other doctrines (novelty, nonobviousness, enablement) rather than categorical exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the statute is broad, practical limits on overbroad business-method patents have often been imposed through other patentability doctrines (e.g., lack of novelty, obviousness, enablement) rather than an outright business-method ban.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that many earlier rejections of business-method patents rested on grounds such as lack of novelty or being mere abstractions; it suggests that, in practice, the legal system often uses these other doctrinal tools to police claims rather than a categorical exclusion. This is guidance for evaluators to consider multiple doctrinal axes when assessing claims.
